title: Surely There Is a God Who Judges
superscription: For the choirmaster. To the tune of "Do Not Destroy." A Miktam of David.

verses.text: Do you indeed speak justly, O rulers? Do you judge uprightly, O sons of men?
No, in your hearts you devise injustice; with your hands you mete out violence on the earth.
The wicked are estranged from the womb; the liars go astray from birth.
Their venom is like the venom of a snake, like a cobra that shuts its ears,
refusing to hear the tune of the charmer who skillfully weaves his spell.
O God, shatter their teeth in their mouths; O LORD, tear out the fangs of the lions.
May they vanish like water that runs off; when they draw the bow, may their arrows be blunted.
Like a slug that dissolves in its slime, like a woman's stillborn child, may they never see the sun.
Before your pots can feel the burning thorns— whether green or dry— He will sweep them away.
The righteous will rejoice when they see they are avenged; they will wash their feet in the blood of the wicked.
Then men will say, "There is surely a reward for the righteous! There is surely a God who judges the earth!"

context.author: The title names David. In Book Two, Psalms 51-65 are all “of David,” and several titles tie them to events in his life.
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship in Jerusalem, and every reader who prays
context.setting: “Do you indeed speak justly, O rulers? Do you judge uprightly, O sons of men? No, in your hearts you devise injustice” (vv.1-2). The wicked go astray from birth (v.3). “Their venom is like the venom of a snake, like a cobra that shuts its ears, refusing to hear the tune of the charmer” (vv.4-5). David prays in vivid images: break the lions’ teeth, let them vanish like water that runs off, like a slug that melts, swept away before a cooking pot can feel the fire (vv.6-9). The end: “Then men will say, There is surely a reward for the righteous! There is surely a God who judges the earth!” (v.11).
context.custom: Snake charmers in the ancient Near East claimed to control snakes with music and spells; a snake that would not respond was the most dangerous (Ecclesiastes 10:11; Jeremiah 8:17). Thorns were burned as quick fuel under cooking pots (Ecclesiastes 7:6). Judges sat in the city gate, and a corrupt judge could ruin the poor.
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 59 is titled for the night Saul’s men watched David’s house.
context.timelineBible: The word translated “rulers” (v.1) may also be read “gods,” as in Psalm 82, where God judges the unjust judges. The souls under the altar ask, “How long, O Lord… until You avenge our blood?” (Revelation 6:10). Paul says, “Do not avenge yourselves… for it is written: Vengeance is Mine” (Romans 12:19). The psalm’s harsh images are prayers handing judgment to God.

translation.meaning: To whisper, charm; a snake charmer’s spell.

gospelParallels.note: How long, O Lord, until You avenge our blood?
Vengeance is Mine; I will repay.
Will not God bring about justice for His elect?

otBackground.note: If the snake bites before it is charmed.

overview.summary: David accuses corrupt rulers who are deaf to justice like a cobra to the charmer, asks God to break their power, and looks to the day all will see there is a God who judges.

archaeology.t: Benches in Iron Age gates where judges sat.
Egyptian art shows the cobra as a royal symbol (the uraeus).

overview.discussion: The psalm ends with confidence that “there is surely a God who judges the earth” (v.11). How does that truth help me face injustice?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (1-60 in the app so far). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: David
